summary: Ottawa and Ontario put $8.7 billion into steel, autos and Ring of Fire roads to cope with U.S. tariffs, as the U.S. Embassy accuses Canadian politicians of meddling in the midterms.
body: Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford announced a joint $8.7-billion plan on Wednesday for industries hit by U.S. tariffs [^1][^2]. About $5.2 billion over five years goes to a new steel fund, $2.5 billion over two years helps automakers retool for connected and electric vehicles, and the two governments will each put up to $1 billion into roads to the Ring of Fire, a mineral-rich area in Northern Ontario [^1][^3]. Ottawa will also freeze its emissions standards for new cars at 2026 levels through the 2029 model year [^3]. Carney said the plan would protect about 220,000 jobs and create about 70,000 linked to the Ring of Fire [^2]. "Their approach has changed. So must ours," Carney said of the U.S. [^1]. Ford said that whoever wins the midterms, "we're not going back to the way things were" [^2]. Carney said he spoke with President Donald Trump at length but gave no sign of a trade breakthrough [^1].

Also on Wednesday, the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa accused Canadian politicians of trying to influence American politics before the Nov. 3 midterms. It named Industry Minister Mélanie Joly, over talk of targeting tariffs at Republican states, and Ford, over the anti-tariff Reagan ad Ontario ran last year [^1]. Carney and Ford rejected the claim; Ford said he has "no interest at all" in U.S. elections [^1]. My read: this is a sign of how tense the relationship has become, more than a formal dispute.

After Alberta's referendum, Carney said Ottawa will "not budge" from sustainable immigration levels but did not rule out giving Alberta more say over immigration, modelled on Quebec's deal from the early 1990s [^4]. On prices, Statistics Canada said Monday that inflation rose to 3.1% in September, driven by gasoline, up 27.8% from a year ago; excluding gas, prices rose 2.2% [^5]. The Bank of Canada decides on interest rates Oct. 28.
differences: The two governments present the plan as protecting jobs and building Canadian supply chains [^2][^3]. The reports we read did not include reactions from opposition parties or unions. On the embassy's claim, the AP notes the embassy offered no evidence that the actions it named were improper interference [^1].

reads.title: Carney says Trump's tariffs hurt Americans as US Embassy alleges Canadian interference
reads.summary: A short, clear account of the $8.7-billion plan, what is in it, and the new U.S. Embassy accusations, with the background on how trade talks broke down.
